\title{A no-go theorem and a bounded exclusion of exceptional points in the
massive scalar spectrum of doubly rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
holes}

% NOT FOR SUBMISSION until these fields are supplied.  REVTeX expands the
% author block eagerly, so plain text is used rather than a formatting macro.
\author{AUTHOR NAME NOT ASSIGNED}
\email{corresponding.author@NOT-ASSIGNED}
\affiliation{AFFILIATION NOT ASSIGNED. ORCID NOT ASSIGNED.}

\date{\today}

\begin{abstract}
We ask whether the enhanced symmetry of the equal-spin surface organizes
defective (exceptional) degeneracies in the massive scalar quasinormal spectrum
of the asymptotically flat, doubly rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
hole. Our first result is exact. Because $\partial_\phi$ and $\partial_\psi$
remain Killing for arbitrary rotation parameters, the quasinormal pencil admits
an invariant decomposition into azimuthal sectors $(m_1,m_2)$, and the Jordan
chains of such a decomposition are the union of the chains of its summands. A
coincidence of frequencies drawn from distinct sectors therefore cannot by
itself create defectiveness: any Jordan chain of length greater than one must
already occur within a single fixed sector. Through the Keldysh expansion of the
resolvent this statement is equivalent to the assertion that such a coincidence
cannot raise the order of the ringdown Green-function pole above one, so it has
direct observational content. The equal-spin multiplets, whose members carry
distinct $(m_1,m_2)$, are accordingly protected from \emph{hybridization}: their
frequencies may and do separate as parameters vary, but they cannot coalesce
into a shared defective block. A residual Klein four-group acting on parameters
\emph{and} sector labels renders diagonal sectors $m_1=m_2$ exactly even in the
spin asymmetry $\delta$; when the associated discriminant curve crosses
$\delta^2=0$ transversally, the physical exceptional branches must occur in
mirror pairs and terminate quadratically on the equal-spin surface. Our second
result is numerical and explicitly bounded. Searching the one channel the
theorem leaves open --- collisions between distinct $(\ell,N)$ branches inside a
fixed sector --- over an atlas of $50\,558$ continued modes in seven sectors, we
find no exceptional point within the declared domain, where the minimum
separation between tracked branches is $0.5116$ in units of the inverse horizon
scale and the eigenvalue condition number remains finite at
$8.73\times10^{3}$. The ten tightest candidates are classified as avoided
crossings by argument-principle, monodromy and Puiseux tests. The searched
domain lies entirely outside the superradiant regime, every tracked mode
exceeding the critical frequency $m_1\Omega_a+m_2\Omega_b$ by at least $1.07$.
We emphasize that this is an exclusion within a declared domain: higher
overtones, higher angular branches, the superradiant regime, and the
quasiresonant regime --- where no recurrence-free solver is applicable --- were
not searched.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%=========================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Defective degeneracies and their observational content}
\label{sec:intro:eps}

Quasinormal modes are the resonances of a black hole: the poles of the retarded
Green function of the perturbation operator, and the observable content of the
ringdown~\cite{Kokkotas1999D46,Berti2009D47,Konoplya2011D48,Bertietal2025D50}.
Because the governing operator is not self-adjoint --- energy leaks through the
horizon and out to infinity --- its spectral theory admits structures with no
Hermitian counterpart. The sharpest of these is the \emph{exceptional point}
(EP): a value of the external parameters at which two or more eigenvalues
\emph{together with their eigenvectors} coalesce, so that the generator becomes
defective and cannot be diagonalized~\cite{KatoE71,Bergholtz2019E63,%
Ashida2020E64}.

The physical consequences are not decorative. If the perturbation problem is
written as a holomorphic operator pencil $T(\omega)$, the Keldysh expansion of
the resolvent about an eigenvalue $\omega_0$ carrying a Jordan chain of length
$q$ produces a pole of order exactly $q$ (Appendix~\ref{app:keldysh}). Inverse
Laplace transformation then yields a time-domain response
\begin{equation}\label{eq:secular}
  \psi(t) \;\sim\; \Big(A_0 + A_1 t + \dots + A_{q-1}t^{q-1}\Big)
  e^{-\ii\omega_0 t},
\end{equation}
so that at an EP2 the ringdown acquires a secular $t\,e^{-\ii\omega_0 t}$
term~\cite{PanossoMacedoetal2025B30,Motohashi2024B24}, the quasinormal expansion
ceases to be a basis, and the excitation factors of the participating modes
diverge individually while their sum stays finite. In the neighbourhood of an
EP2 the eigenvalues respond to a perturbation of size $\epsilon$ as
$\Ord(\epsilon^{1/2})$ rather than $\Ord(\epsilon)$, which is the same
square-root sensitivity that drives the pseudospectral instability of black-hole
spectra~\cite{Jaramillo2020C36,Jaramillo2021C37,Destounisetal2021C38}. For
black-hole spectroscopy this matters directly: overtone-resolved ringdown fits
presuppose a discrete, diagonalizable spectrum, and the presence of a nearby
exceptional structure would invalidate that presupposition rather than merely
perturb it.

Such structures are by now documented across black-hole perturbation theory.
Branching of quasinormal modes was identified for nearly extremal
Kerr~\cite{Yangetal2012B18}; eigenvalue repulsions organize the Kerr--Newman
spectrum and connect the Kerr and Reissner--Nordstr\"om
families~\cite{Diasetal2021B19,Dias2022B20,Davey2023B21}; genuine exceptional
points, hysteresis, and ergodic spectral flow appear for massive scalars on
Kerr~\cite{Cavalcante2024B22,Cavalcante2024B23,Cavalcante2025B29}; and the
resonant excitation associated with near-degenerate pairs has been analysed in
detail~\cite{Oshita2025B25,Yang2025B26,Kubota2025B27,Caoetal2025B28,%
Wang2026B32}. Most directly relevant here, continuous \emph{exceptional lines}
have been established for massive scalars on Kerr--de Sitter and
Myers--Perry--de Sitter, where the near-Nariai limit reduces the radial problem
to P\"oschl--Teller form and permits a semi-analytic
treatment~\cite{Nakamoto2026A17,Daveyetal2022A13,Ponglertsakul2020A12}.

The non-Hermitian literature supplies the counting that organizes the search.
An EP2 is the vanishing of a complex discriminant, hence two real conditions:
codimension two. A one-parameter family therefore meets exceptional points only
accidentally, a two-parameter family meets them at isolated points, and a
three-parameter family meets them along curves~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}. Symmetry
modifies this counting: parity--time or generalized chiral symmetry reduces the
codimension of \emph{higher-order} points, making third-order points generic in
two parameters rather than the four otherwise
required~\cite{Mandal2021E65}, and symmetry can protect entire exceptional
chains in lattice models~\cite{Zhangetal2022E66}.

\subsection{Why five-dimensional Myers--Perry}\label{sec:intro:why}

The five-dimensional Myers--Perry black hole~\cite{Myers1986A01,Emparan2008A02}
is an unusually favourable laboratory for asking whether that machinery has a
gravitational realization. Four features make it so.

First, the massive Klein--Gordon equation separates exactly for arbitrary $a$
and $b$~\cite{Murata2007A03,Wu2008A04}, a property extending to Dirac and
massive vector fields~\cite{Wu2008A04,Frolovetal2018A09}, so the spectral
problem reduces to a coupled pair of ordinary differential equations rather than
a genuinely two-dimensional eigenvalue problem.

Second, the massive scalar spectrum with two arbitrary spins has been
computed~\cite{Huang2025A16,Lietal2023A15,Lu2023A14}, including the long-lived
branches that appear when $\mu$ becomes comparable to the inverse horizon scale,
so a numerical baseline exists.

Third, the parameter space has \emph{exactly} the dimension at which
codimension-two sets become generic. The background supplies two independent
rotation parameters and the field supplies a mass, giving the three real
parameters $(s,\delta,\mu)$ defined below. Four-dimensional Kerr, by contrast,
offers only $(a,\mu)$, so exceptional points there are isolated rather than
curves. If symmetry-organized exceptional structure exists anywhere in
asymptotically flat black-hole perturbation theory, this is where the counting
says it should be easiest to find.

Fourth, and decisively for the question we ask, the isometry group is enhanced
when the two angular momenta coincide,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:enhancement}
  \mathbb{R}\times U(1)\times U(1)\ \longrightarrow\
  \mathbb{R}\times SU(2)\times U(1),
\end{equation}
and the metric becomes cohomogeneity-one~\cite{Murata2008A06}. Equation
\eqref{eq:enhancement} produces exact degeneracies in the perturbation spectrum,
and the equal-spin surface is a symmetric locus embedded in the
three-dimensional parameter space --- precisely the configuration in which one
expects symmetry-protected exceptional structure to appear.

Higher-dimensional rotating black holes are of interest in their own right, as
the arena in which black-hole uniqueness fails, as the setting of the
Gregory--Laflamme and ultraspinning
instabilities~\cite{Diasetal2010A07,Emparan2014A08}, and through the large-$D$
expansion. Our motivation here is more specific: we use the system as a
controlled setting in which the parameter counting is favourable and an exact
symmetry statement is available, and we regard the methodological conclusions of
Secs.~\ref{sec:local} and~\ref{sec:results} as transferable to the
four-dimensional problem.

\subsection{Statement of results}\label{sec:intro:results}

The natural expectation, and the standard mechanism in non-Hermitian
systems~\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, is that the degeneracies created
by \eqref{eq:enhancement} unfold into exceptional points once the symmetry is
broken by $\delta\ne0$. We show that this expectation fails, and that it fails
for an exact reason.

We claim the following. (i) An exact structural theorem
(Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo}): a coincidence of frequencies from distinct azimuthal
sectors cannot by itself produce a Jordan chain, hence cannot raise the order of
the ringdown Green-function pole. (ii) An exact symmetry classification
(Table~\ref{tab:stabilizers}), with a conditional termination law for
diagonal-sector exceptional loci (Proposition~\ref{prop:termination}). (iii) A
\emph{bounded} numerical exclusion of exceptional points within an explicitly
declared parameter domain, Eq.~\eqref{eq:domain}. Claim (iii) is not a statement
about the system as a whole: overtones $N>3$, angular branches beyond those
listed, the region $s>0.45$ or $\mu>1.8$, the superradiant regime, and the
quasiresonant regime lie outside it, and we make no claim there.

The paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} fixes the
geometry and its thermodynamics. Section~\ref{sec:separated} derives the
separated system, its singular structure, and the flux identity that defines the
superradiant regime. Section~\ref{sec:nogo} proves the sector decomposition and
the no-go theorem. Section~\ref{sec:group} classifies the residual symmetry.
Section~\ref{sec:local} develops the local spectral theory and establishes which
diagnostics are admissible --- a question on which we found two natural choices
to be inadmissible. Section~\ref{sec:numerics} describes the numerical
formulations, Sec.~\ref{sec:atlas} the atlas, and Sec.~\ref{sec:results} the
exclusion. Sections~\ref{sec:quasi}--\ref{sec:astro} treat the quasiresonant
limit and the observational implications, and Sec.~\ref{sec:limits} the
limitations.

%=========================================================================
\section{Background geometry and horizon thermodynamics}\label{sec:background}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Metric and horizons}\label{sec:bg:metric}

In Boyer--Lindquist-like coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)$ with
$\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ and $\phi,\psi\in[0,2\pi)$, signature $(-++++)$, the
Myers--Perry metric with two rotation parameters reads
\begin{align}\label{eq:metric}
  \dd s^2 =\ & -\dd t^2
    + \frac{M}{\Sigma}\Big(\dd t - a\sin^2\!\theta\,\dd\phi
      - b\cos^2\!\theta\,\dd\psi\Big)^{\!2} \nonumber\\
    &+ \frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}\,\dd r^2 + \Sigma\,\dd\theta^2 \nonumber\\
    &+ (r^2+a^2)\sin^2\!\theta\,\dd\phi^2
     + (r^2+b^2)\cos^2\!\theta\,\dd\psi^2 ,
\end{align}
with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigmapi}
  \Sigma = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\!\theta + b^2\sin^2\!\theta,\quad
  \Pi = (r^2+a^2)(r^2+b^2),
\end{equation}
and $\Delta=(\Pi-Mr^2)/r^2$. Here $M$ is the Myers--Perry mass parameter, of
dimension $(\text{length})^2$, \emph{not} the scalar mass $\mu$; we set $M=1$,
which fixes the length unit, and we verify
$\sqrt{|g|}=r\,\Sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta$ as a check on the symbolic
derivation. The ADM mass and angular momenta are
$M_{\rm ADM}=3\pi M/8$, $J_\phi = \tfrac{2}{3}M_{\rm ADM}\,a$,
$J_\psi = \tfrac{2}{3}M_{\rm ADM}\,b$.

With $z=r^2$ the horizon polynomial is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizonpoly}
  P(z) = (z+a^2)(z+b^2) - Mz = (z-z_+)(z-z_-),
\end{equation}
whence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zpm}
  z_\pm = \tfrac12\Big[(M-a^2-b^2)\pm\sqrt{(M-a^2-b^2)^2-4a^2b^2}\Big],
\end{equation}
with $z_+z_-=a^2b^2$ and $z_++z_-=M-a^2-b^2$. A horizon exists iff
$M\ge(|a|+|b|)^2$, and we use
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extremality}
  \mathcal{E}\equiv M-(|a|+|b|)^2
\end{equation}
as the extremality measure, $\mathcal{E}=0$ at extremality. Note that
\eqref{eq:zpm} implies $z_-\le M/4$ for any sub-extremal configuration, so the
inner horizon radius satisfies $r_-\le\tfrac12\sqrt M$; we quote $r_-$ rather
than $z_-$ throughout, since a domain restriction on one is a different
restriction on the other.

Throughout we use the adapted rotation coordinates
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sdelta}
  s=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad \delta=\frac{a-b}{2},
\end{equation}
so $\delta=0$ is the equal-spin surface on which \eqref{eq:enhancement} holds
and $s=0$ is the counter-rotating surface $a=-b$.

\subsection{Horizon thermodynamics}\label{sec:bg:thermo}

The horizon generators are $\xi=\partial_t+\Omega_a\partial_\phi
+\Omega_b\partial_\psi$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizondata}
  \Omega_a = \frac{a}{z_++a^2},\qquad
  \Omega_b = \frac{b}{z_++b^2},
\end{equation}
and the surface gravity and Hawking temperature are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kappa}
  \kappa = \frac{r_+\,(z_+-z_-)}{(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2)},
  \qquad T_H = \frac{\kappa}{2\pi}.
\end{equation}
The horizon is a squashed three-sphere of area
\begin{equation}\label{eq:area}
  \mathcal{A} = \frac{2\pi^2}{r_+}\,(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2),
  \qquad S_{\rm BH}=\frac{\mathcal{A}}{4},
\end{equation}
which reduces to $\mathcal{A}=2\pi^2r_+^3$ and $T_H=1/(2\pi r_+)$ in the
Schwarzschild--Tangherlini limit $a=b=0$; both limits are verified numerically.
Table~\ref{tab:thermo} records these quantities at the corners of the searched
domain. The temperature varies by only $30\%$ across the domain while the
horizon angular velocity ranges from zero to $0.68$, so the domain is a
rotation-dominated rather than temperature-dominated slice of parameter space.

%=========================================================================
\section{The separated system}\label{sec:separated}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Separation}\label{sec:sep:separation}

With the mode ansatz
\begin{equation}\label{eq:modeansatz}
  \Phi = e^{-\ii\omega t + \ii m_1\phi + \ii m_2\psi}\,R(r)\,S(\theta),
  \qquad m_1,m_2\in\mathbb{Z},
\end{equation}
the equation $(\Box-\mu^2)\Phi=0$ separates exactly. Since
$\Phi\propto e^{-\ii\omega t}$, damped modes have $\Imm\,\omega<0$. The angular
equation is
\begin{align}\label{eq:angular}
  \frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}&\frac{\dd}{\dd\theta}
  \left[\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\frac{\dd S}{\dd\theta}\right]
  + \Big[\Lambda + (\omega^2-\mu^2)\big(a^2\cos^2\!\theta \nonumber\\
  &+b^2\sin^2\!\theta\big)
    - \frac{m_1^2}{\sin^2\!\theta} - \frac{m_2^2}{\cos^2\!\theta}\Big]S = 0 ,
\end{align}
and the radial equation
\begin{align}\label{eq:radial}
  \frac{1}{r}\frac{\dd}{\dd r}&\!\left[r\Delta\frac{\dd R}{\dd r}\right]
  + \Big[\frac{W^2}{r^4\Delta} - \frac{G^2}{r^2} - (a^2+b^2)\omega^2 \nonumber\\
  &+ 2\omega(am_1+bm_2) - \mu^2r^2 - \Lambda\Big]R = 0 ,
\end{align}
with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:WG}
  W = \Pi\,\omega - m_1a(r^2+b^2) - m_2b(r^2+a^2),\quad
  G = ab\,\omega - am_2 - bm_1 .
\end{equation}
The separation constant is normalized by $\Lambda=\ell(\ell+2)$ at $a=b=0$. We
re-derived \eqref{eq:angular}--\eqref{eq:WG} symbolically from
\eqref{eq:metric} in exact rational arithmetic rather than transcribing them,
and the derivation is re-executed as an automated test; the route is given in
Appendix~\ref{app:sep}.

\subsection{The angular problem and two exactly degenerate surfaces}
\label{sec:sep:angular}

Substituting $u=\cos^2\!\theta$ in \eqref{eq:angular} converts it to a
Jacobi-type equation on $u\in[0,1]$ with regular singular points at $u=0,1$ and
an irregular point at infinity. Writing
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ahatc2}
  \hat A \equiv \Lambda + (\omega^2-\mu^2)b^2,\qquad
  c^2 \equiv (\omega^2-\mu^2)(a^2-b^2),
\end{equation}
the problem becomes a five-dimensional spheroidal problem of the type
classified in Ref.~\cite{Berti2005A05}, with $c^2$ the spheroidicity and $\hat A$
the eigenvalue. Because $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)=4s\delta$, one has the exact
identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2exact}
  \boxed{\;c^2 = 4\,s\,\delta\,(\omega^2-\mu^2)\;}
\end{equation}
which is not perturbative. Three consequences follow immediately.

\emph{(i)} On $\delta=0$ the spheroidicity vanishes identically for
\emph{every} $s$, $\mu$ and $\omega$. The angular operator is then the round
Laplacian on $S^3$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lambdaround}
  \hat A = \ell(\ell+2),\qquad \ell = 2n+|m_1|+|m_2|,\ n\ge0 ,
\end{equation}
and the full $(\ell+1)^2$-fold $SO(4)$ degeneracy.

\emph{(ii)} The same holds on $s=0$, the counter-rotating configuration
$a=-b$. This is a \emph{second} exactly degenerate surface, unrelated to
\eqref{eq:enhancement}, and the two intersect transversally at the origin of
the $(s,\delta)$ plane.

\emph{(iii)} The angular degeneracy is lifted only by the \emph{product}
$s\delta$, so the leading splitting of an $SO(4)$ multiplet is
$\Ord(s\delta)$ rather than $\Ord(\delta)$.

Moreover, at $\delta=0$ the radial equation \eqref{eq:radial} and the horizon
condition depend on $(m_1,m_2)$ only through
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mtotal}
  m = m_1+m_2 ,
\end{equation}
which is the algebraic origin of the multiplet structure of
Sec.~\ref{sec:nogo:multiplets}.

\subsection{Singular structure of the radial equation}\label{sec:sep:singular}

In the variable $z=r^2$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:radial} has apparent singularities at
$z=0$ and $z=z_\pm$ and an irregular singular point at infinity. The point
$z=0$ is only apparent: using $W(0)=abG$ and $P(0)=a^2b^2$, the would-be $1/z$
terms cancel identically whenever $ab\ne0$, so $z=0$ is an \emph{ordinary}
point. The equation is therefore of confluent Heun type, with exactly two
regular singular points and one irregular point of rank one at infinity.

At $z=z_+$ the indicial equation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:indicial}
  \varrho^2+\sigma_+^2 = 0,\qquad \varrho=\pm\ii\sigma_+ ,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigmaplus}
  \sigma_+ = \frac{\omega-m_1\Omega_a-m_2\Omega_b}{2\kappa}
  \equiv \frac{\omega-\omega_c}{2\kappa},
\end{equation}
where the second equality defines the \emph{critical frequency}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:omegac}
  \omega_c \equiv m_1\Omega_a + m_2\Omega_b .
\end{equation}
Equation \eqref{eq:sigmaplus} follows from the factorization
$W(z_+)=(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2)(\omega-\omega_c)$, itself a consequence of
\eqref{eq:WG} and \eqref{eq:horizondata}. The quasinormal condition selects the
ingoing branch $\varrho=-\ii\sigma_+$.

At large $r$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:radial} reduces to
$R''+\tfrac3r R'+\big(\Omega^2+\Ord(r^{-2})\big)R=0$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Omegadef}
  \Omega \equiv \sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2},
\end{equation}
so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:infinityBC}
  R \sim e^{\pm\ii\Omega r}\,r^{-3/2}\big(1+\Ord(r^{-1})\big).
\end{equation}
The exponent $-3/2$ is exact and there is \emph{no} Coulomb phase: because
$D-3=2$ the radial potential is an even function of $r$ and possesses no $1/r$
tail. This is a structural difference from four-dimensional massive Kerr, where
a logarithmic phase $\propto\mu^2 M\log r$
appears~\cite{DetweilerD53,Dolan2007D55}, and it simplifies both the asymptotic
matching and the continued-fraction construction of Sec.~\ref{sec:numerics}.
Details are in Appendix~\ref{app:frobenius}.

\subsection{Flux identity and the superradiant regime}\label{sec:sep:flux}

Equation \eqref{eq:radial} can be written in formally self-adjoint form
$(r\Delta R')'+r\,V(r)R=0$. For \emph{real} $\omega$ and $\mu$ the potential $V$
is real, so the Wronskian-like quantity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wronskian}
  \mathcal{W}[R] = r\Delta\big(\bar R R' - R\bar R'\big)
\end{equation}
is independent of $r$. Evaluating \eqref{eq:wronskian} on a scattering solution
that is ingoing at the horizon and a superposition of incoming and outgoing
waves at infinity gives the standard flux balance
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fluxbalance}
  |\mathcal{R}|^2 = 1 - \frac{\sigma_+}{\;\Omega\,}\;
  \frac{(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2)}{\;\;}\Big/ \mathcal{N},
\end{equation}
with $\mathcal{N}>0$ a positive normalization depending only on the asymptotic
amplitudes. The sign of the transmitted flux is therefore the sign of
$\sigma_+$, i.e.\ of $\omega-\omega_c$: for
\begin{equation}\label{eq:superradiance}
  0 < \omega < \omega_c = m_1\Omega_a+m_2\Omega_b
\end{equation}
the reflected flux exceeds the incident flux and the mode extracts rotational
energy from the black hole. This is the five-dimensional, two-spin analogue of
Zel'dovich--Misner superradiance, and for a massive field it is the mechanism
underlying superradiant bound-state
instabilities~\cite{Ponglertsakul2020A12,Lietal2023A15}.

Two remarks matter for what follows. First, the entire searched domain lies
\emph{outside} \eqref{eq:superradiance}: across the eleven branches tracked in
Sec.~\ref{sec:quasi} the smallest value of $\Rem\,\omega-\omega_c$ is $+1.07$,
attained in sector $(1,1)$ where $\omega_c\le0.51$ while
$\Rem\,\omega\ge1.51$. Every mode we compute is consequently damped, as
observed, and our exclusion says nothing about the superradiant sector. Second,
$\sigma_+$ changes sign across \eqref{eq:superradiance}, so the horizon boundary
condition \eqref{eq:sigmaplus} changes character there; a search in that regime
would require the boundary condition to be re-derived rather than continued.

\subsection{The quasinormal problem as an operator pencil}
\label{sec:sep:pencil}

Equations \eqref{eq:angular}--\eqref{eq:radial} with the boundary conditions
\eqref{eq:sigmaplus} and \eqref{eq:infinityBC} define a \emph{nonlinear}
eigenvalue problem: $\omega$ enters the coefficients, and $\Lambda$ is itself a
function of $\omega$. We write it abstractly as a holomorphic operator pencil
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pencil}
  T(\omega)\,u = 0 ,
\end{equation}
and record the coupled scalar form used numerically,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Fdef}
  F\big(\omega;\,s,\delta,\mu,\,m_1,m_2,\ell\big)=0,
  \qquad \Lambda=\Lambda(\omega;\dots),
\end{equation}
in which $\Lambda$ is recomputed at every evaluation. Freezing $\Lambda$ while
differentiating with respect to $\omega$ discards
$\partial_\Lambda F\cdot\dd\Lambda/\dd\omega$ and is a standard route to
spurious exceptional points; all derivatives here are total.

%=========================================================================
\section{Sector decomposition and the no-go theorem}\label{sec:nogo}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{The torus action}\label{sec:nogo:torus}

No component of \eqref{eq:metric} depends on $\phi$ or $\psi$, so
$\partial_\phi$ and $\partial_\psi$ are Killing for \emph{arbitrary} $a,b$ ---
not merely on the equal-spin surface --- and the torus
$T^2=S^1_\phi\times S^1_\psi$ acts by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:torusaction}
  (\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}u)(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)
  = u(t,r,\theta,\phi-\alpha,\psi-\beta).
\end{equation}
Quasinormal eigenfunctions are not square integrable --- by
\eqref{eq:infinityBC} they diverge at infinity whenever $\Imm\,\omega<0$ --- so
a Fourier decomposition justified in $L^2(T^2)$ is not available. We therefore
avoid $L^2$ entirely and work from the group action, stating the hypotheses
explicitly, since they are what the argument consumes.

\begin{proposition}[Invariant sector decomposition]\label{prop:decomp}
Let $X$ be a Banach space carrying the pencil $T(\omega)$, and suppose
\begin{itemize}
\item[(H1)] $\{\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}\}$ is a uniformly bounded, strongly
continuous representation of $T^2$ on $X$;
\item[(H2)] $T(\omega)$ and all its $\omega$-derivatives commute with every
$\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}$, and the domain of $T(\omega)$ is
$\mathcal{R}$-invariant.
\end{itemize}
Then the isotypic projections
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projectors}
  \Pi_{m_1m_2} = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\iint
  e^{-\ii(m_1\alpha+m_2\beta)}\,\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}\,
  \dd\alpha\,\dd\beta
\end{equation}
are bounded, mutually orthogonal idempotents commuting with $T(\omega)$, and
they separate points:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:separating}
  \Pi_{m_1m_2}u=0\ \ \forall\,(m_1,m_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ u=0 .
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The integral \eqref{eq:projectors} converges as a Bochner integral by (H1), with
$\|\Pi_{m_1m_2}\|\le\sup_{\alpha\beta}\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}\|$.
Idempotence and mutual orthogonality follow from the group law and the
orthogonality of the characters of $T^2$. Commutation with $T$ and its
derivatives is (H2). For \eqref{eq:separating}, let $K_N$ denote the
two-dimensional Fej\'er kernel, a nonnegative approximate identity on $T^2$, and
set
\begin{equation}
  \sigma_N u = \iint K_N(\alpha,\beta)\,\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}u\,
  \dd\alpha\,\dd\beta ,
\end{equation}
a finite positive combination of the $\Pi_{m_1m_2}u$ with weights
$\big(1-\tfrac{|m_1|}{N+1}\big)\big(1-\tfrac{|m_2|}{N+1}\big)$. Strong
continuity and the approximate-identity property give $\sigma_Nu\to u$ in norm.
If every $\Pi_{m_1m_2}u$ vanishes then $\sigma_Nu=0$ for all $N$, hence $u=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:whatweuse}
We deliberately do \emph{not} assert that the Fourier series of $u$ converges,
nor that $X$ is an unconditional direct sum of isotypic subspaces; in a general
Banach representation neither is automatic, and neither is needed. Only
boundedness, commutation and \eqref{eq:separating} enter the argument, and all
three follow from (H1)--(H2) by Fej\'er summation. Hypotheses (H1)--(H2) hold in
the standard realizations of the quasinormal problem --- weighted spaces adapted
to \eqref{eq:infinityBC}, and the hyperboloidal
realization~\cite{Jaramillo2020C36} --- because \eqref{eq:torusaction} relabels
two \emph{compact} coordinates, acts by isometries of \eqref{eq:metric}, touches
neither $r$ nor $\theta$, and leaves \eqref{eq:sigmaplus} and
\eqref{eq:infinityBC} invariant, the horizon exponent depending only on the
sector's own labels. The decomposition is over $(m_1,m_2)$ \emph{only} and does
not use separation of variables in $\theta$; see Sec.~\ref{sec:nogo:survives}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Jordan chains and the order of the resolvent pole}
\label{sec:nogo:jordan}

\begin{definition}
A tuple $(v_0,\dots,v_{q-1})$ with $v_0\ne0$ is a Jordan chain of length $q$ for
the holomorphic pencil $T$ at $\omega_*$ if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jordanchain}
  \sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{1}{i!}\,T^{(i)}(\omega_*)\,v_{j-i}=0,
  \qquad j=0,\dots,q-1 .
\end{equation}
The eigenvalue is \emph{semisimple} if every chain has length one and
\emph{defective} otherwise; an EP of order $q$ is a parameter value at which the
maximal chain length is $q\ge2$.
\end{definition}

By the Keldysh expansion (Appendix~\ref{app:keldysh}), the maximal chain length
at $\omega_*$ equals the order of the pole of $T(\omega)^{-1}$ there, hence by
\eqref{eq:secular} the degree of the secular polynomial in the ringdown. The
following lemma therefore has direct physical content.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:directsum}
Under Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp}, every Jordan chain of $T$ at $\omega_*$
projects componentwise onto Jordan chains of the sector restrictions
$T_{m_1m_2}$, at least one of which is nontrivial and of the same length;
conversely a chain in one sector extends by zero. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maxchain}
  \max_{\text{chains of }T}q
  \;=\;\max_{(m_1,m_2)}\ \max_{\text{chains of }T_{m_1m_2}}q .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply the bounded projector $\Pi_{m_1m_2}$ to the $j$-th equation of
\eqref{eq:jordanchain}. Commutation with every $T^{(i)}$ gives the identical
relation for the projected components, so
$(\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_0,\dots,\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_{q-1})$ is a chain in that sector. By
\eqref{eq:separating}, $v_0\ne0$ forces $\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_0\ne0$ for at least one
sector, whose chain then has length $q$. The converse is immediate, and
\eqref{eq:maxchain} follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cross-sector no-go]\label{thm:nogo}
A coincidence of quasinormal frequencies belonging to \emph{distinct} azimuthal
sectors cannot by itself create defectiveness. Any Jordan chain of length
greater than one at $\omega_*$ must already occur within a single fixed
$(m_1,m_2)$ sector. Equivalently, such a coincidence cannot raise the order of
the pole of $T(\omega)^{-1}$, hence cannot produce a secular term in
\eqref{eq:secular}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:directsum} and Appendix~\ref{app:keldysh}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The wording is chosen so as not to exclude the case in which two sectors share a
frequency while one of them independently contains an exceptional point. There
$T$ is defective, but the defectiveness belongs to the single sector and owes
nothing to the coincidence. The underlying algebra is standard~\cite{KatoE71};
what is specific here is that Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp} holds for
\emph{all} $a,b$, so the conclusion is not confined to the symmetric locus.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The equal-spin multiplets}\label{sec:nogo:multiplets}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:multiplet}
On the equal-spin surface the labels degenerate at fixed $(\ell,m)$ form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:multipletset}
  \mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}=\big\{(m_1,m_2): m_1+m_2=m,\ |m_1|+|m_2|\le\ell,
\end{equation}
$\ell-|m_1|-|m_2|\in2\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\big\}$, with
$|\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}|=\ell+1$ independently of $m$; summing over the $\ell+1$
admissible $m$ gives $(\ell+1)^2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $m\ge0$ put $m_1=m-m_2$. The value $|m_1|+|m_2|=m$ is attained for
$m_2\in[0,m]$, that is $m+1$ pairs, while each value $m+2j$ with $j\ge1$ is
attained by exactly two pairs, $m_2=m+j$ and $m_2=-j$. The constraint in
\eqref{eq:multipletset} admits $j\le(\ell-m)/2$, whence
$|\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}|=(m+1)+2\cdot\tfrac{\ell-m}{2}=\ell+1$, independent of
$m$. The case $m<0$ follows from the parity generator of
Sec.~\ref{sec:group}. The admissible $m$ are $-\ell,-\ell+2,\dots,\ell$, so the
level total is $(\ell+1)^2$, the dimension of the $SO(4)$ scalar harmonic level
consistent with \eqref{eq:Lambdaround}.
\end{proof}

By \eqref{eq:mtotal} the members of $\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}$ share the same radial
problem at $\delta=0$ and are exactly degenerate there; they carry distinct
$(m_1,m_2)$ and therefore lie in distinct sectors. By Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo}
that coincidence cannot hybridize into a shared defective block at any $\delta$.
It is essential to state what this does \emph{not} say: the frequencies are free
to separate, and they do. Figure~\ref{fig:multiplet} shows the sectors $(1,1)$
and $(2,0)$, which share $m=2$, meeting at $\delta=0$ and separating for
$\delta\ne0$, the splitting being $\Ord(s\delta)$ as \eqref{eq:c2exact}
requires. The protection is against hybridization, not against splitting.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_multiplet.pdf}
  \caption{Sectors $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$ share $m=m_1+m_2=2$ and are exactly
  degenerate on the equal-spin surface, separating for $\delta\ne0$ ($\ell=2$,
  $N=0$, $s=0.20$, $\mu=0.6$). By Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo} the coincidence at
  $\delta=0$ cannot by itself be defective; the branches nevertheless split
  freely as $\delta$ varies.}
  \label{fig:multiplet}
\end{figure}

\subsection{What survives}\label{sec:nogo:survives}

Within a single sector, distinct angular branches $\ell$ are \emph{not} separate
summands: $\Lambda_j(\omega)$ depends on $\omega$, so they are branches of one
analytic family and Lemma~\ref{lem:directsum} does not apply to them. This is
why Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp} was established without invoking separation of
variables: a decomposition taken over $(m_1,m_2,\ell)$ would have proved too
much, and would have been false. Collisions between distinct $(\ell,N)$ branches
inside a fixed sector are the surviving channel, and the rest of the paper
addresses them.

%=========================================================================
\section{Residual symmetry and a conditional termination law}\label{sec:group}
%=========================================================================

Two exact transformations act on the pair (parameters, sector labels),
\begin{align}
  E:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(b,a,m_2,m_1), \label{eq:Egen}\\
  P:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(-a,-b,-m_1,-m_2), \label{eq:Pgen}
\end{align}
where $E$ interchanges the labels of the two rotation planes and $P$ is the
orientation reversal $\phi\to-\phi$, $\psi\to-\psi$ composed with reversal of
both rotation senses. Both leave \eqref{eq:metric} and
\eqref{eq:angular}--\eqref{eq:WG} invariant for arbitrary $a,b,\mu$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:klein}
  G=\{1,E,P,EP\}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2 ,
\end{equation}
acting in adapted coordinates as $E:(s,\delta)\mapsto(s,-\delta)$,
$P:(s,\delta)\mapsto(-s,-\delta)$, $EP:(s,\delta)\mapsto(-s,\delta)$.

The essential observation is that \emph{no element of $G$ acts on the parameters
alone}: each also moves the sector. A symmetry of the parameter space \emph{at
fixed sector} therefore exists only in sectors stabilized by the corresponding
element, as collected in Table~\ref{tab:stabilizers}. In particular the
convenient assertion that exceptional sets come in quadruples under independent
reflections $s\to-s$ and $\delta\to-\delta$ holds only in the sector $(0,0)$.

\begin{table}[b]
\centering
\begin{ruledtabular}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
sector & stabilizer & induced symmetry \\
\colrule
$m_1=m_2$ & $E$ & $\omega(s,\delta)=\omega(s,-\delta)$ \\
$m_1=-m_2$ & $EP$ & $\omega(s,\delta)=\omega(-s,\delta)$ \\
$(0,0)$ & $G$ & even in $\delta$ and in $s$ \\
generic & $\{1\}$ & none \\
\end{tabular}
\end{ruledtabular}
\caption{Stabilizers and the induced parameter symmetries. All three nontrivial
cases are verified numerically below $10^{-12}$, with a negative control
confirming that a generic sector is \emph{not} even in $\delta$ (Supplemental
Material).}
\label{tab:stabilizers}
\end{table}

In a diagonal sector every branch is even in $\delta$, hence --- granted
analyticity in the parameters --- an analytic function of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tdef}
  t\equiv\delta^2 .
\end{equation}
Let $\omega_\pm$ denote two interacting branches and define the discriminant
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ddef}
  D\equiv(\omega_+-\omega_-)^2 .
\end{equation}
Then $D$ depends on $\delta$ only through $t$, and an EP2 is $D=0$: two real
conditions, the familiar codimension two~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}, defining a
curve in $(s,t,\mu)$. The physical parameter space, however, is the double cover
$\delta=\pm\sqrt t$, which exists only for $t\ge0$.

\begin{proposition}[Mirror pairing and conditional termination]
\label{prop:termination}
Assume analyticity in the parameters and let $\Gamma$ be a component of
$\{D=0\}$ in $(s,t,\mu)$. The physical locus is invariant under $E$, so
exceptional branches occur in mirror pairs. If in addition $\Gamma$ meets $t=0$
\emph{transversally}, passing into $t<0$, then parametrizing $\Gamma$ by
arclength $\tau$ with $t\approx c\tau$, $c\ne0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrtlaw}
  \delta=\pm\sqrt{c\,\tau},
\end{equation}
so the two mirror branches meet at $\delta=0$ and terminate, approaching the
equal-spin surface quadratically rather than crossing it.
\end{proposition}

The termination is conditional on transversality: a tangential crossing, or a
component remaining in $t>0$, is not excluded. This is the mechanism by which
the equal-spin symmetry constrains exceptional topology here --- not by
protecting a degeneracy, that channel being closed by Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo},
but by constraining the \emph{unfolding}. It is the analogue of the
symmetry-constrained exceptional structures catalogued in non-Hermitian lattice
models~\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, differing in that symmetry there
lowers the codimension of higher-order points, whereas here it acts on the
reality structure of the unfolding parameter. The prediction was recorded before
the numerical search and remains untested, no exceptional locus having been
found to exhibit it.

%=========================================================================
\section{Local spectral theory and admissible diagnostics}\label{sec:local}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Normal form, Newton polygon and Puiseux expansion}
\label{sec:local:puiseux}

Two interacting branches are described locally by a $2\times2$ non-Hermitian
generator $H(\bm p)$. Its individual entries are not observable, since any
similarity transformation alters them, but the two symmetric functions are:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:TD}
  T=\omega_++\omega_-=\operatorname{tr}H,\qquad
  D=(\operatorname{tr}H)^2-4\det H .
\end{equation}
The eigenvalues are $\omega_\pm=\tfrac12(T\pm\sqrt D)$, so an EP2 is exactly
$D=0$. Writing the characteristic equation as
$\mathcal{P}(\omega,t)=\omega^2-T\omega+\det H=0$ near a simple zero of $D$ along
a transversal direction $t$, the Newton polygon of $\mathcal{P}$ has a single
segment of slope $1/2$, and the branches admit the Puiseux expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:puiseux}
  \omega_\pm(t)=\omega_*+c_1t\pm c_{1/2}t^{1/2}+c_{3/2}t^{3/2}+\Ord(t^2),
\end{equation}
with $c_{1/2}\ne0$~\cite{KatoE71,Nennig2019E67}. Three observable signatures
follow, and we use all three:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the splitting obeys $|\omega_+-\omega_-|\simeq2|c_{1/2}|t^{1/2}$, against
$\Ord(t)$ at an ordinary crossing and a nonzero constant at an avoided crossing;
\item continuing the pair once around a small loop encircling the EP interchanges
the branches, and two circuits restore them, so the monodromy is the
transposition of $S_2$;
\item the argument principle counts two zeros inside a contour that shrinks with
the candidate.
\end{enumerate}
For an EP of order $q$ the Newton polygon has slope $1/q$, the splitting scales
as $t^{1/q}$, and the monodromy is a $q$-cycle.

\subsection{Two inadmissible diagnostics}\label{sec:local:inadmissible}

Because the conclusion of Sec.~\ref{sec:results} is negative, the admissibility
of each diagnostic must be established rather than assumed. We record two
natural choices that are \emph{not} admissible.

\emph{The derivative of the spectral condition.} $F$ in \eqref{eq:Fdef} is
determined only up to a nonvanishing holomorphic factor: Leaver's continued
fraction may be rescaled, or inverted at a different depth, without changing its
zeros. Under $F\mapsto gF$ one has $\tilde F'(\omega_1)=g(\omega_1)F'(\omega_1)$
at a simple root, so $|\dd F/\dd\omega|$ has no invariant meaning and cannot
bound the distance to an exceptional point.

\emph{The ratio of leading Taylor coefficients.} Expanding
$F=\sum_ka_k(\omega-\omega_1)^k$ about a simple root, $|a_1/a_2|$ approximates
the distance to a nearby second root. It fails as a bound for two independent
reasons. First, it is only \emph{asymptotically} insensitive to normalization:
writing $g=g_0+g_1(\omega-\omega_1)+\dots$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:a1a2distortion}
  \frac{\tilde a_1}{\tilde a_2}
  = \frac{a_1/a_2}{1+(g_1/g_0)(a_1/a_2)},
\end{equation}
so the distortion is $\Ord(|g'/g|\,d)$ with $d$ the separation. This is
measurable: for $g=Ae^{k\omega}$ the observed ratio follows $|1+kd|^{-1}$ to five
decimals, from $1.0003$ at $d=10^{-4}$ to $1.43$ at $d=0.1$
[Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}(a)]. Second, and decisively, $|a_1/a_2|$ measures the
distance to the nearest zero \emph{or pole}. Leaver's continued fraction is
meromorphic, and contour integration about our tightest candidate returns
$\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{P}=0$ at every radius out to $0.20$: one zero and one pole
enclosed. The small values returned are pole distances and carry no spectral
meaning. We therefore \emph{withdraw} this estimator as a bound and retain it
only as a local indicator.

What survives is admissible because it is built from eigenvalue differences of
independently verified modes: the pairwise separation between tracked branches,
each confirmed by an ODE residual of order $10^{-12}$ and by cross-solver
agreement; and the eigenvalue condition number
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kappa}
  \kappa=\frac{\|u\|\,\|v\|}{|v^\dagger T'(\omega_*)u|},
\end{equation}
computed from Solver~C's collocation matrix, which is free of the continued
fraction's poles. By the Keldysh expansion, $\kappa^{-1}\propto|v^\dagger T'u|$
is precisely the residue normalization of the simple pole, so $\kappa\to\infty$
is the analytic signature of an approaching EP. We note also that the
discriminant \eqref{eq:Ddef} is \emph{not} independent evidence, being the
square of the separation.

\subsection{The verification gate}\label{sec:local:gate}

A detector that has never been shown to fire cannot support a negative result.
All routines were calibrated on problems whose exceptional structure is known in
closed form --- $\lambda^2-t$ (EP2), $\lambda^3-t$ (EP3),
$\lambda^2-(t^2+g^2)$ (avoided crossing), Jordan blocks, and block-diagonal
coincidences --- and, equally importantly, on \emph{negative controls} in which
the detector must not fire [Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}(b)]. Roots are recovered
from contour moments by Newton's identities, requiring no starting
guess~\cite{KravanjaVanBarel2000}. A candidate is accepted only if it satisfies
every applicable condition of Table~\ref{tab:gate}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\begin{ruledtabular}
\begin{tabular}{cll}
& condition & ten tightest \\
\colrule
G1 & separation $\to0$ under refinement & \textbf{fail} \\
G2 & argument-principle count $=2$ & pass \\
G3 & both roots found without a guess & pass \\
G4 & monodromy interchanges the branches & \textbf{fail} \\
G5 & two circuits restore the assignment & --- \\
G6 & splitting $\sim t^{1/2}$, preferred over $t^1$ & \textbf{fail} \\
G7 & Jordan chain solvable, geom.\ $<$ alg. & --- \\
G8 & stable under resolution/depth/precision & --- \\
G9 & confirmed by a recurrence-free solver & --- \\
G10 & inside the validated solver domain & pass \\
\end{tabular}
\end{ruledtabular}
\caption{The EP2 gate. G2 and G3 are \emph{preconditions}: they establish only
that two distinct roots lie near one another, which is what makes a point a
candidate. The decisive evidence is G1, G4 and G6, which fail uniformly. For an
EP3 one additionally requires three coalescing branches, count $3$,
$a_1=a_2=0$ with $a_3\ne0$, cube-root splitting, and a three-cycle monodromy.}
\label{tab:gate}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_calibration.pdf}
  \caption{(a) The coefficient ratio is only asymptotically insensitive to the
  normalization of the spectral condition: its distortion under
  $F\mapsto10^{7}e^{3\omega}F$ follows $|1+(g'/g)d|^{-1}$ exactly, reaching
  $43\%$ at $d=0.1$, whereas the enclosed zero count is unaffected. (b) The
  Puiseux exponent separates an EP2 ($t^{1/2}$) from an ordinary crossing
  ($t^{1}$) and from an avoided crossing, which saturates at a constant.}
  \label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

%=========================================================================
\section{Numerical formulation}\label{sec:numerics}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Leaver's method}\label{sec:num:leaver}

Factoring the boundary behaviour of Sec.~\ref{sec:sep:singular} out of
\eqref{eq:radial},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:leaveransatz}
  R = (z-z_+)^{-\ii\sigma_+}(z-z_-)^{\xi}e^{\ii\Omega r}r^{-3/2}
  \sum_{n\ge0}a_n\Big(\frac{z-z_+}{z-z_-}\Big)^{\!n},
\end{equation}
and clearing denominators yields a linear recurrence with polynomial
coefficients~\cite{Leaver1985D51,LeaverD52},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:recurrence}
  \sum_{j=0}^{p}c_j(n)\,a_{n-j}=0 ,
\end{equation}
of width $p+1=13$ for generic two-spin parameters, collapsing to $9$ in the
static case. Gaussian elimination reduces \eqref{eq:recurrence} to three terms,
$\alpha_na_{n+1}+\beta_na_n+\gamma_na_{n-1}=0$, and the quasinormal condition ---
that the \emph{minimal} solution be selected --- becomes the vanishing of a
continued fraction,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cf}
  \beta_N-\frac{\alpha_{N-1}\gamma_N}{\beta_{N-1}-}\cdots
  =\frac{\alpha_N\gamma_{N+1}}{\beta_{N+1}-}
   \frac{\alpha_{N+1}\gamma_{N+2}}{\beta_{N+2}-}\cdots
\end{equation}
We stress a point that cost us: the inversion index $N$ changes the conditioning
of \eqref{eq:cf} and, at finite depth, its zero set. At a tracked $N=2$ root the
$N=2$ inversion gives $|F|=1.9\times10^{-13}$ while inversions $0,1,3$ give
$7\times10^{-2}$, $1\times10^{-1}$ and $1.1$, values unchanged from depth $200$
to depth $3200$. Every quantity extracted from the wrong inversion is void, and
a residual gate now enforces the correct choice.

\subsection{Large-$n$ asymptotics}\label{sec:num:tail}

The convergence of \eqref{eq:cf} is governed by the large-$n$ behaviour of
$R_n=a_n/a_{n-1}$. Writing the characteristic equation of
\eqref{eq:recurrence} as $A(1/R)=0$, the root $x=1$ has multiplicity at least
five in $A$ and exactly four in the neighbouring coefficient polynomials, so the
integer-power ansatz degenerates and half-integer powers survive:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail}
  R_n = 1+u_1n^{-1/2}+u_2n^{-1}+\Ord(n^{-3/2}),\quad
  u_1=-\sqrt{-2c},
\end{equation}
with $c=\ii\Omega(r_+-r_-)$ and the sign fixed by minimality. Including the
leading term reduces the depth required for a given accuracy by a factor
$\approx1.35$, worth $1.4$ digits at depth $200$. Higher coefficients are
unavailable: the Gaussian reduction degrades beyond $n\sim500$--$800$, where the
backward ratio recursion collapses onto a spurious, problem-independent
$R_n-1=2/n$. See Appendix~\ref{app:frobenius}.

\subsection{Exterior complex scaling}\label{sec:num:scaling}

An independent formulation rotates the radial contour beyond a matching radius,
$r=r_m+\varsigma e^{\ii\vartheta}$, $\varsigma\in[0,L]$, and discretizes
\eqref{eq:radial} by Chebyshev collocation. The outgoing solution
\eqref{eq:infinityBC} decays along the contour provided
\begin{equation}\label{eq:anglecondition}
  \tan\vartheta > -\frac{\Imm\,\Omega}{\Rem\,\Omega},
\end{equation}
defining a minimum admissible angle $\vartheta_{\min}$. Under this
transformation a genuine resonance becomes an eigenvalue of the scaled operator
and is independent of $\vartheta$, whereas the rotated continuum sweeps with
$\vartheta$; the construction thus separates resonances from artifacts without
any root finder. Condition \eqref{eq:anglecondition} is decisive in
Sec.~\ref{sec:quasi}.

\subsection{Solvers, domains and benchmarks}\label{sec:num:domains}

Four solvers are used, in two families sharing no discretization
(Table~\ref{tab:solvers}). Any claim requires agreement between the families;
two implementations wrapping one discretization are not independent evidence.
Related matrix and spectral methods are reviewed
in~\cite{Hatsuda2021D49,Choetal2011D57,Lin2016D58,Linetal2017D59,%
Matyjasek2017D60,Fortuna2020D62}, with open implementations for Kerr
in~\cite{Stein2019D61}.

\centering

& formulation & rec.-free & domain \\
\colrule
A & Leaver continued fraction & no & $r_-\le0.2287$ \\
B & raw recurrence, Hill, Wynn & no & as A \\
C & exterior complex scaling & yes & as A, $\vartheta_{\min}<90^\circ$ \\

The five-dimensional Schwarzschild--Tangherlini fundamental scalar mode is
reproduced to all twelve published digits,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:st5d}
  \omega = 0.533835574268-0.383375368513\,\ii\qquad(r_+=1),
\end{equation}
with absolute error $5.0\times10^{-13}$ against Ref.~\cite{Matyjasek2021} and
$2.2\times10^{-12}$ between Solvers~A and~B. The exchange symmetry
$(a,m_1)\leftrightarrow(b,m_2)$ holds numerically to $4.2\times10^{-15}$, and
three solvers agree below $10^{-5}$ on ten benchmark points. The atlas domain
extends to $r_-=0.2287$, beyond the previously validated $r_-\le0.19$; Solvers~A
and~C agree to at most $2.06\times10^{-9}$ on nine spanning points including the
domain corners, which is the evidence supporting that extension.

%=========================================================================
\section{The branch atlas}\label{sec:atlas}
%=========================================================================

Branches are identified by continuation history, never by sorting frequencies:
at an avoided crossing two branches exchange order in $\Rem\,\omega$ while
remaining distinct modes. Each step is seeded by quadratic extrapolation in an
arclength parameter and accepted only if the predictor miss
$\varepsilon_{k+1}=|\omega_{k+1}-\omega^{\rm pred}_{k+1}|$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:misstest}
  \varepsilon_{k+1}\le\max\!\Big(4\,\mathrm{med}\{\varepsilon_1,..,\varepsilon_k\},\,
  0.02\max(|\omega_{k+1}|,1)\Big).
\end{equation}
The first argument is essential: the predictor miss is a local truncation error
and follows a smooth trend along a genuine branch, so a jump appears as a sudden
multiple of the running median. A tolerance proportional to $|\omega|$ alone is
a \emph{constant}, and at $|\omega|\approx3.7$ it admitted a jump in which the
trend of $\Imm\,\omega$ reversed; the contaminated point became, until detected,
the tightest reported candidate.

The atlas comprises $50\,558$ points over the seven independent sectors
$(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(-1,-1)$, $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$, with
$\ell\in\{\ell_{\min},\ell_{\min}+2,\ell_{\min}+4\}$, $\ell_{\min}=|m_1|+|m_2|$,
and $N=0,\dots,3$, over
\begin{equation}\label{eq:domain}
  s\le0.42,\ \ |\delta|\le0.20,\ \ \mu\le1.8,\ \
  r_-\le0.2287,\ \ \mathcal{E}\ge0.294 .
\end{equation}
The remaining sectors $(0,1)$, $(0,2)$, $(1,2)$ are images of $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$,
$(2,1)$ under $E$ and are spot-checked rather than recomputed. The maximum
continued-fraction residual is $3.6\times10^{-9}$; $118$ predictor-miss and $33$
non-convergence events are recorded rather than filled in, and four
branch-label collapses are excluded and counted.

Two predictions of Secs.~\ref{sec:nogo}--\ref{sec:group} are recovered from
independently computed frequencies as an end-to-end check, having been imposed
nowhere:
\begin{align}
  \big|\,|\omega_i-\omega_j|_{+\delta}-|\omega_i-\omega_j|_{-\delta}\big|
    &\lesssim10^{-12}, \label{eq:check1}\\
  \big|\,\text{gap}_{(1,1)}-\text{gap}_{(2,0)}\big|_{\delta=0}
    &= 9\times10^{-12}. \label{eq:check2}
\end{align}

%=========================================================================
\section{The bounded exclusion}\label{sec:results}
%=========================================================================

Within the domain \eqref{eq:domain},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bound}
  \min_{\text{atlas}}|\omega_i-\omega_j| = 0.5116,
  \qquad \kappa_{\max}=8.73\times10^{3},
\end{equation}
the latter against $\kappa=18.3$ at an ordinary control mode. An EP2 requires
the separation to vanish and, by \eqref{eq:kappa} and the Keldysh expansion,
$\kappa$ to diverge; neither occurs. The minimum separation is $\approx0.51$
where $|\omega|\approx2$--$4$, a relative separation of order $15\%$, and it is
attained on the \emph{boundary} of \eqref{eq:domain}, at $s=0.42$,
$\delta=-0.20$, $\mu=1.8$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:exclusion}).

The ten tightest candidates were put through the gate of
Table~\ref{tab:gate}. All ten are rejected with a common signature: two distinct
roots are present, but there is no coalescence, no monodromy interchange, and no
$t^{1/2}$ splitting. The classification is therefore \emph{avoided crossing} ---
the behaviour familiar from eigenvalue repulsion in the Kerr--Newman
family~\cite{Diasetal2021B19,Davey2023B21}, here without the accompanying
exceptional points. Consistently, the elevated but finite
$\kappa=8.73\times10^{3}$ is what one expects at a genuine avoided crossing: by
\eqref{eq:kappa} it is a factor $476$ above the control value, whereas an
approaching EP2 would show $\kappa\sim d^{-1}$ with $d\to0$.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_exclusion.pdf}
  \caption{The bounded exclusion. (a) Level curves of the separation between the
  $N=2$ and $N=3$ branches at $\ell=4$ in sector $(1,1)$, on the equal-spin
  surface; the star marks the global minimum, which lies on the boundary of the
  searched domain (heavy axes). (b) Distribution of the tracked separation over
  the atlas. No claim is made outside the domain \eqref{eq:domain}.}
  \label{fig:exclusion}
\end{figure}

%=========================================================================
\section{The quasiresonant limit}\label{sec:quasi}
%=========================================================================

As $\mu$ grows, branches migrate toward the threshold $\omega^2=\mu^2$ and
become arbitrarily long lived, the five-dimensional analogue of the
quasiresonances of massive fields on rotating
backgrounds~\cite{Ponglertsakul2020A12,Lietal2023A15,Huang2025A16}. Tracking
eleven branches across six sectors with an adaptive step, the damping falls
through $8.6$ orders of magnitude along a single continuous branch, from
$0.357$ at $\mu=0$ to $8.65\times10^{-10}$ at $\mu=2.968$, with
$\Rem\,\omega\to\mu$. This is a branch point in $\mu$, not a coalescence: the
neighbouring overtone remains at $-\Imm\,\omega\sim0.1$ throughout, so the
branches separate rather than merge. Every walk terminates where double
precision can no longer resolve the mode, so the reported minima are lower
bounds on how far a branch was followed, not infima.

Because $\Rem\,\omega\to\mu$ from above while $\omega_c\le0.51$ in these
sectors, the quasiresonant branches move \emph{away} from the superradiant
condition \eqref{eq:superradiance} as $\mu$ grows. The long-lived modes we track
are therefore not incipient superradiant instabilities, and the mechanism that
would produce a genuine instability --- a quasi-bound state with
$\Rem\,\omega<\omega_c$, requiring $\mu$ small and $\omega_c$ large --- lies
outside \eqref{eq:domain}.

The same regime settles a question about solver behaviour that proves to be
physics rather than numerics. By \eqref{eq:anglecondition}, as
$\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ the outgoing wave ceases to oscillate and becomes a pure
growing exponential, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:anglelimit}
  \vartheta_{\min}\longrightarrow90^\circ
  \qquad\text{as}\qquad \Rem\,\Omega\to0,
\end{equation}
and \emph{no admissible contour exists}. We measure
$\vartheta_{\min}=89.92^\circ$ and $89.81^\circ$ at the two points where the
recurrence-free solvers fail, against $4.4^\circ$ at an ordinary near-extremal
point where they succeed. Equation \eqref{eq:anglelimit} is a limit of the
\emph{formulation}, not a convergence failure: no increase of resolution,
precision or domain decomposition removes it, which is why a multidomain
refinement of the near-horizon region --- which resolves $r_+-r_-$ by
construction --- did not help. It follows that difficulty in this range is
controlled by $\mu$ and \emph{not} by proximity to extremality: ordinary modes
continue smoothly to $\mathcal{E}=0.0103$ with residuals $\sim10^{-13}$ over
thirty-seven consecutive steps.

%=========================================================================
\section{Observational and astrophysical context}\label{sec:astro}
%=========================================================================

The system studied here is not itself an astrophysical object. Its relevance is
methodological and structural, and we state the connection carefully rather than
overstate it.

First, the observational stakes of exceptional structure lie in ringdown
spectroscopy. Multimode fits to a post-merger signal presuppose a discrete,
diagonalizable spectrum with well-separated overtones; by \eqref{eq:secular} an
exceptional point replaces two exponentials by $(A+Bt)e^{-\ii\omega_*t}$, and
near one the individual excitation factors diverge while the total response
stays finite, so that fitted amplitudes become
ill-conditioned~\cite{Motohashi2024B24,Oshita2025B25,Kubota2025B27}. Any
programme that tests the no-hair theorem by extracting several damped
exponentials therefore has a stake in whether exceptional points occur at
accessible parameters, and in whether symmetry generates them systematically.

Second, our negative result speaks to a specific mechanism. The natural
conjecture --- that an enhanced isometry produces degeneracies which unfold into
exceptional points --- is exactly what Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo} forbids whenever
the degenerate modes are distinguished by conserved azimuthal quantum numbers.
The theorem is not special to five dimensions: it uses only that the background
possesses two commuting azimuthal Killing fields that survive the symmetry
breaking. In four-dimensional Kerr the corresponding statement, with the single
Killing field $\partial_\phi$, forbids exceptional points between modes of
different $m$; the exceptional points that are found in massive-scalar
Kerr~\cite{Cavalcante2024B22,Cavalcante2024B23} are, consistently,
within a single $m$ sector. Searches for symmetry-protected exceptional
structure should therefore be directed at within-sector overtone collisions
rather than at multiplet degeneracies.

Third, higher-dimensional rotating black holes are of interest as the setting
where uniqueness fails and where ultraspinning and Gregory--Laflamme
instabilities operate~\cite{Diasetal2010A07,Emparan2014A08}. Our domain
\eqref{eq:domain} is far from the ultraspinning regime --- it is bounded by
$\mathcal{E}\ge0.294$, whereas the relevant instabilities set in near
extremality --- so the modes studied here are stable, damped, and non-superradiant
throughout, as Table~\ref{tab:thermo} and Sec.~\ref{sec:sep:flux} confirm.

%=========================================================================
\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
%=========================================================================

The exclusion is bounded, and we state the boundaries plainly. The minimum lies
on the edge of \eqref{eq:domain}; a targeted probe beyond it finds the
separation falling to $0.472$ at $s=0.45$ but rising again at $\mu=3.0$ and
$3.6$, so the trend does not extrapolate to zero --- yet no claim is made for
$s>0.45$ or $\mu>1.8$. Overtones $N>3$ and higher $\ell$ were not searched, and
highly damped overtones are known to be
delicate~\cite{Nollert1996C33,Miyachi2025C45}. The superradiant regime
\eqref{eq:superradiance} was not searched, and there the horizon boundary
condition changes character. The quasiresonant regime was not searched, since by
\eqref{eq:anglelimit} no recurrence-free solver is applicable and the
evidentiary standard of Table~\ref{tab:gate} cannot be met; this is the one
region of the studied sectors in which an exceptional point could still be
hiding.

Certification was attempted and is limited in
scope~\cite{MooreE73,TuckerE74,Breiding2020E69,Duff2024E70}: we obtain a
Krawczyk certificate for finite-dimensional systems and an Arb ball enclosure of
the angular eigenvalue of the truncated Jacobi matrix, validated by recovering
$\ell(\ell+2)$ at $c^2=0$. The radial problem is \emph{not} certified, its
recurrence coefficients being extracted by a discrete Fourier transform for which
we have no rigorous aliasing bound, so the truncation term in
\begin{equation}\label{eq:errorbudget}
  E_{\rm total}\le E_{\rm disc}+E_{\rm trunc}+E_{\rm arith}+E_{\rm root}
\end{equation}
cannot be bounded. No truncated-recurrence or continuum certificate is claimed.

Finally, the numerical result is an exclusion over a declared domain, not a
theorem, and must not be conflated with Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo}, which is exact.

%=========================================================================
\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
%=========================================================================

We exclude exceptional points within the declared numerical domain; we do not
claim their absence from the system. Exceptional lines \emph{do} occur in the de
Sitter members of this family~\cite{Nakamoto2026A17}, and the present
$\Lambda=0$ result is a contrast between spacetimes rather than a contradiction:
the de Sitter mechanism relies on the cosmological horizon and the
P\"oschl--Teller reduction, neither of which has an asymptotically flat
analogue, and the accompanying eigenvalue
repulsions~\cite{Daveyetal2022A13} are likewise a de Sitter phenomenon.

Within the asymptotically flat doubly rotating case the structure is sharply
organized. The most natural route to exceptional behaviour is closed exactly, by
the same symmetry that generates the candidate degeneracies. The surviving route
is numerically weak in the region searched: those branches repel with a
separation never falling below half a unit. Since the parameter space has
exactly the dimension at which codimension-two sets should be
generic~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}, their absence in this region is informative
rather than expected.

Two methodological points may outlive the application. First, neither the
derivative of a spectral condition nor the ratio of its leading Taylor
coefficients is an admissible bound on the distance to an exceptional point: the
former is not invariant under the renormalization freedom, and the latter
measures the distance to the nearest zero \emph{or pole} of a meromorphic
condition. Second, a small computed separation between two \emph{labels} is
evidence about the labels before it is evidence about the physics.

The natural next step is a hyperboloidal formulation, the only method that
remains applicable as $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ and therefore the only route into the
quasiresonant regime~\cite{Jaramillo2020C36,PanossoMacedoetal2025B30}, together
with an extension into the superradiant sector, where the boundary condition
must be re-derived and where a genuine instability, rather than an exceptional
point, is the object of interest.

%=========================================================================
\section{Separation of the massive Klein--Gordon equation}\label{app:sep}
%=========================================================================

With the ansatz \eqref{eq:modeansatz}, the equation
$\partial_\nu(\sqrt{|g|}g^{\nu\rho}\partial_\rho\Phi)=\mu^2\sqrt{|g|}\Phi$
requires the inverse metric. Rather than inverting the full $5\times5$ matrix,
note that \eqref{eq:metric} is block diagonal: the pair $(r,\theta)$ is
diagonal, and the remaining $(t,\phi,\psi)$ block is $3\times3$. Inverting the
small block and using $\sqrt{|g|}=r\Sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta$ gives the wave
operator in closed form.

Substituting $u=\cos^2\!\theta$ converts the result into a rational function of
$(r,u)$, at which point exact cancellation is tractable. Writing the separation
quotient as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sepquotient}
  Q(r,u)=\frac1R\,\mathcal{L}_rR+\frac1S\,\mathcal{L}_uS,
\end{equation}
separability is the statement $\partial^2Q/\partial r\,\partial u\equiv0$, which
we verify in exact rational arithmetic. Partial fractions in $u$ then isolate
the angular operator, giving \eqref{eq:angular}; the remainder is
\eqref{eq:radial}. Two checks are applied: $\sqrt{|g|}$ must equal
$r\Sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta$ identically, and at $a=b=\mu=0$, $m_1=m_2=0$ the
radial bracket must reduce to $\omega^2r^4/(r^2-M)-\Lambda$ with
$\Lambda=\ell(\ell+2)$.

%=========================================================================
\section{Frobenius exponents and the asymptotic tail}\label{app:frobenius}
%=========================================================================

\emph{Horizon.} Near $z=z_+$, retaining the leading behaviour of
$W^2/(r^4\Delta)$ in \eqref{eq:radial} gives the indicial equation
\eqref{eq:indicial}. The factorization
$W(z_+)=(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2)(\omega-\omega_c)$, which follows from \eqref{eq:WG}
and \eqref{eq:horizondata}, is what puts $\sigma_+$ in the form
\eqref{eq:sigmaplus}; the quasinormal condition selects $-\ii\sigma_+$.

\emph{Infinity.} At large $r$ the equation becomes
$R''+\tfrac3rR'+(\Omega^2+\Ord(r^{-2}))R=0$. Because the potential is even in
$r$ there is no $\Ord(1/r)$ term, so the WKB exponent contains no logarithm and
\eqref{eq:infinityBC} follows, the outgoing branch being selected. The absence
of a Coulomb phase distinguishes this problem from four-dimensional massive
Kerr.

\emph{Tail.} Setting $R_n=a_n/a_{n-1}$ in \eqref{eq:recurrence} and substituting
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tailansatz}
  a_n\sim\exp\!\Big(\lambda\sqrt n+\eta\log n+d_1n^{-1/2}+d_2n^{-1}+\cdots\Big)
\end{equation}
shows that the characteristic polynomial $A(1/R)$ has $x=1$ as a root of
multiplicity at least five, while the neighbouring coefficient polynomials have
multiplicity exactly four. The balance at order $n^{-3/2}$ reads $-u_1A'(1)=0$
with $A'(1)=0$, so the integer-power series degenerates and half-integer powers
survive, giving \eqref{eq:tail}. Two independent numerical confirmations are
available: the scaling test, in which $(R_n-1)\sqrt n$ converges while
$(R_n-1)n$ diverges, and the depth signature $\exp(-k\sqrt N)$ of the truncation
error.

%=========================================================================
\section{Keldysh expansion and the ringdown pole order}\label{app:keldysh}
%=========================================================================

Let $T(\omega)$ be holomorphic and Fredholm of index zero near $\omega_*$, with
a single eigenvalue there. If $\omega_*$ is \emph{simple}, with right and left
null vectors $u,v$ normalized by $v^\dagger T'(\omega_*)u=1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:keldysh1}
  T(\omega)^{-1}=\frac{u\,v^\dagger}{\omega-\omega_*}+\Ord(1),
\end{equation}
a first-order pole whose residue is the rank-one spectral projector. More
generally, if the canonical system of root functions at $\omega_*$ has maximal
chain length $q$, the Keldysh theorem gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:keldyshq}
  T(\omega)^{-1}=\sum_{k=1}^{q}\frac{\mathcal{S}_k}{(\omega-\omega_*)^{k}}
  +\Ord(1),
\end{equation}
with $\mathcal{S}_q\ne0$ built from the chain vectors. The order of the pole is
therefore exactly the maximal Jordan-chain length.

The retarded Green function of the perturbation problem is
$G(\omega)=T(\omega)^{-1}$ acting on the source, and the time-domain response is
its inverse Laplace transform. A pole of order $k$ at $\omega_*$ contributes
$t^{k-1}e^{-\ii\omega_*t}/(k-1)!$, giving \eqref{eq:secular}. Combining with
Lemma~\ref{lem:directsum}: since the maximal chain length of $T$ equals the
maximum over sectors, and a cross-sector coincidence contributes no chain longer
than those already present in the individual sectors, such a coincidence cannot
raise the pole order and cannot produce a secular term. This is the precise
sense in which Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo} has observational content.

Equation \eqref{eq:keldysh1} also explains the role of \eqref{eq:kappa}: the
normalization $v^\dagger T'(\omega_*)u$ is the residue denominator, so
$\kappa\propto|v^\dagger T'u|^{-1}$ diverges precisely when the residue of the
simple pole blows up, i.e.\ as two simple poles merge into a double one.
